items.question: On which side of the road do vehicles drive in Malawi?
options: The right-hand side
The left-hand side
Either side, as long as you are careful
The middle of the road
items.explanation: Malawi drives on the left. Keep to the left-hand side of the road unless you are overtaking or turning.

items.question: What must you do at a red, eight-sided (octagonal) STOP sign?
options: Slow down and continue if the road looks clear
Stop only if other traffic is coming
Come to a complete stop, then go only when it is safe
Hoot and proceed
items.explanation: A STOP sign always requires a complete stop at the line, even when the road looks empty. Move off only when it is safe.

items.question: Road signs shaped as a triangle with a red border usually…
options: Give an order you must obey
Warn you of a hazard ahead
Give directions to a town
Show a parking area
items.explanation: Triangular signs with a red border are warning signs — for example a sharp bend, a school or a pedestrian crossing ahead.

items.question: Round signs with a red border usually…
options: Tell you what you must NOT do
Give information about services
Warn you about road works
Show the route to a hospital
items.explanation: Circular signs with a red ring are prohibitory — e.g. no entry, no overtaking or a speed limit.

items.question: A pedestrian is waiting to cross at a zebra crossing. What should you do?
options: Speed up to pass before they step out
Hoot to warn them to wait
Slow down and stop to let them cross
Flash your lights and drive on
items.explanation: Be ready to stop and give way to pedestrians at a zebra crossing. Never wave or hoot them across — another vehicle might not stop.

items.question: What is a safe minimum following distance behind the vehicle in front on a dry road?
options: Half a second
At least a two-second gap
One car length at any speed
As close as possible so others can't cut in
items.explanation: Leave at least a two-second gap in good conditions, and at least double that on wet or dusty roads.

items.question: How does a wet road affect your stopping distance?
options: It makes no difference
It becomes shorter
It can be up to twice as long
Only heavy vehicles are affected
items.explanation: Tyres have less grip on wet roads, so stopping distances can double. Slow down and leave a bigger gap.

items.question: A traffic light changes from green to steady amber as you approach. What should you do?
options: Accelerate to get through before red
Stop, unless you are so close that stopping would be unsafe
Hoot and continue
Stop immediately, even if a vehicle is right behind you
items.explanation: Amber means stop. Only continue if you have already crossed the stop line or are so close that stopping could cause a collision.

items.question: When should you use your indicators?
options: Only when a police officer is present
In good time before changing direction or lane
After you have finished turning
Only at night
items.explanation: Signal clearly and early so other road users know what you intend to do — then check it is safe before you move.

items.question: Before moving off from the side of the road, you should…
options: Check your mirrors and blind spot, and signal if needed
Just check the rear-view mirror
Hoot and pull out quickly
Rely on other drivers to let you in
items.explanation: Mirrors alone don't show everything. Look over your shoulder to check the blind spot before you pull out.

items.question: What is a vehicle's 'blind spot'?
options: An area around the car you cannot see in your mirrors
A dark part of the road at night
A spot where parking is prohibited
The area directly in front of the bonnet
items.explanation: Blind spots are areas not covered by your mirrors — usually over your shoulders. Always check them before changing lanes or moving off.

items.question: When driving on the left, on which side should you normally overtake another vehicle?
options: On the left
On the right
On whichever side has more space
On the shoulder of the road
items.explanation: Overtake on the right, and only when you can see the road ahead is clear and it is legal to do so.

items.question: You are dazzled by the headlights of an oncoming vehicle at night. What should you do?
options: Switch on your own full beam
Look towards the left edge of the road and slow down
Close your eyes briefly
Speed up to pass it quickly
items.explanation: Slow down (stop if necessary) and look towards the left-hand edge of the road until your eyes recover.

items.question: An ambulance with flashing lights and a siren is coming up behind you. What should you do?
options: Stop immediately in your lane
Speed up to stay ahead of it
Move over to the left safely and let it pass
Ignore it unless it hoots
items.explanation: Help emergency vehicles get past by moving to the left when it is safe — don't brake suddenly or mount a pavement dangerously.

items.question: When should you use your hazard warning lights?
options: When parking illegally for a short time
When your vehicle has broken down and is causing an obstruction
To thank another driver
When driving in heavy rain
items.explanation: Hazard lights warn others that your vehicle is stationary and a hazard — for example after a breakdown.

items.question: Who in a vehicle should wear a seat belt?
options: Only the driver
Only front-seat passengers
Everyone, wherever seat belts are fitted
Only on long journeys
items.explanation: Seat belts save lives in the front and the back. Make sure every occupant is buckled up before you move off.

items.question: How does alcohol affect your driving?
options: It improves concentration
It slows your reactions and impairs your judgement
It has no effect in small amounts
It only affects night driving
items.explanation: Even small amounts of alcohol slow your reactions and make you over-confident. The safest choice is not to drink at all if you are driving.

items.question: You need to make an urgent phone call while driving. What should you do?
options: Hold the phone between your ear and shoulder
Make the call while driving slowly
Find a safe place, stop, and then make the call
Send a text message instead
items.explanation: Using a phone while driving is a major cause of crashes. Pull over safely and stop before using it.

items.question: You see a warning sign for a school ahead. What should you do?
options: Hoot to warn children
Reduce speed and watch out for children
Keep your speed, the sign is only for weekends
Overtake slower vehicles before the school
items.explanation: Children can be unpredictable. Slow down and be ready to stop near schools.

items.question: Before a long journey, which of these should you check?
options: Tyre pressure and tread
Oil and coolant levels
Lights and indicators
All of the above
items.explanation: A quick check of tyres, fluids and lights before a long trip helps prevent breakdowns and crashes.

items.question: When entering a roundabout, you should normally…
options: Give way to traffic already on the roundabout
Enter quickly before other vehicles
Expect traffic on the roundabout to give way to you
Stop in the middle of the roundabout
items.explanation: Give way to traffic already on the roundabout (coming from your right) unless road markings or signs tell you otherwise.

items.question: Why should you avoid driving when you are very tired?
options: It uses more fuel
Your reactions and concentration are reduced
It is only a problem on motorways
Tiredness has no effect on driving
items.explanation: Fatigue slows reactions like alcohol does. On long trips, take a break at least every two hours.
